title: God's Generosity
theme: Discovering God's generosity in times of uncertainty, learning to be content with what we have, and allowing His blessings to become blessings for others.
opening: When is it enough? When our own needs and desires meet the suffering of someone who has almost nothing, what does faith ask of us? A reflection on gratitude, material blessings, generosity, and Jesus' warning that we cannot serve both God and wealth.
prayer: Heavenly Father,  Thank You for Your generosity throughout this past year. Even in uncertainty, You have sustained us. Even when I was afraid, there was enough to continue.  Forgive me for the times I have been so occupied with what I want that I have overlooked what I already have. Teach me the contentment Paul learned, to remain faithful in both abundance and need. Help me enjoy the blessings You have given me without allowing them to become more important than You.  And Lord, I ask You to look with tenderness upon the woman living in her car, and upon all those who are without shelter, security, or someone to care for them. Help me recognize when I can be of service. Give me courage to respond with kindness, wisdom, and respect.  St. Jude, pray for me as I continue facing financial difficulties. Intercede for those who feel desperate, forgotten, or without hope. Help me trust God's provision and seek His kingdom before all else.  Lord, let my gratitude become generosity. Let my blessings become opportunities to love. And let my heart remain open to those whose burdens are far greater than my own.  Above all, teach me to seek You first.  Amen.
body:
“I know indeed how to live in humble circumstances; I know also how to live with abundance.” — Philippians 4:12  “You cannot serve God and mammon.” — Luke 16:13

This past year, God has been extraordinarily generous to us. I haven't been able to work as I once did, and there have been moments when I truly wondered how we would manage. We have faced unexpected expenses, financial losses, disputes over money, and circumstances that seem to require one more phone call, one more appeal, one more attempt to make things right. And yet, somehow, we have continued to get by.

There have been losses, but there have also been gains. There have been moments of genuine fear, followed by unexpected relief. When I look back, I cannot help but praise God for what we have been given.

I am reminded of the widow of Zarephath in the First Book of Kings. She had only enough flour and oil to prepare what she believed would be her final meal with her son. Yet when the prophet Elijah asked her for food, she trusted his assurance that God would provide. And the flour did not run out. The oil did not run dry.

I have thought about that woman often. God did not fill her house with riches. He provided what she needed to continue, day after day. And perhaps that is what I have been witnessing in my own life. Not an absence of difficulty, but provision in the midst of it.

I have also continued giving to Sierra House, something I feel strongly called to do. Even during periods when I have worried about our own finances, I have been grateful that we could continue helping others.

But lately, another question has been troubling me. How much is enough?

Our house needs work. There are repairs to make, trees to trim, a driveway to improve, a backyard I would love to restore, and changes that would make our home more beautiful and functional. I want these things. I enjoy beauty. I enjoy when things work properly, when a space feels comfortable, when a home is cared for and inviting.

But sometimes I feel guilty for wanting them. I wonder whether a truly spiritual person would be content with what they already have. Would someone who loves God more deeply be less concerned about a beautiful yard or a renovated bathroom?

And then I think about a woman I've seen living in her car near a park.

I've only seen her vehicle a few times. The windows are dark, and a towel covers the driver's door. I don't know her name, her circumstances, or what has brought her there. But I cannot forget her.

I have a house that I want to improve, while she may be struggling simply to find a safe place to sleep. Suddenly, my wishes seem terribly small. How can I be thinking about landscaping when someone else is living in a vehicle? How can I want more when another person has so little?

These are uncomfortable questions, but I don't want to turn away from them.

In today's first reading, Paul tells the Philippians that he has learned to live with both abundance and need. He has experienced hunger and plenty. He knows what it means to have enough and what it means to go without. But what interests me most is that he says he has learned to live in these circumstances.

Contentment was something he came to understand, perhaps through hardship, dependence on others, and his growing trust in Christ. He tells us, “I have the strength for everything through him who empowers me.” Paul's strength wasn't the assurance that he would always have enough money, food, or comfort. It was his relationship with Christ.

And yet Paul doesn't dismiss material generosity. He thanks the Philippians for sharing in his distress and supporting him. Their gifts mattered because they were an expression of love. Our material resources can serve something far greater than ourselves.

Then, in today's Gospel, Jesus says something that makes me uncomfortable in a different way: “You cannot serve God and mammon.”

I have been thinking about what it actually means to serve money. Is it wrong to want to improve my home? Is it wrong to ask St. Jude to intercede for me when I am struggling with financial disputes? Is it wrong to hope that money owed to us might be recovered, or that an insurance company might reconsider a denial?

I don't believe those desires are necessarily wrong. But I am beginning to recognize that there is a difference between using money and allowing money to govern my heart.

I can pursue what is fair. I can care for the home God has allowed us to have. I can enjoy beautiful things. But can I remain at peace when I cannot have them? Can I accept waiting? And, perhaps more importantly, can I recognize when someone else's need deserves more attention than my own wishes?

I think about the woman in her car. I haven't spoken with her. I don't even know whether she is still there. Part of me wants to approach her, but I don't want to frighten her or draw attention that might make her situation more difficult. Still, I feel a desire to do something, and perhaps that desire is worth listening to.

I don't think I am being asked to feel ashamed of having a home. But I do think I am being asked to remember that my blessings carry responsibilities. What good is a beautiful home if I become so occupied with improving it that I no longer see the person struggling outside its walls? And what good is financial security if it makes me less willing to share?

I have been praying often to St. Jude, asking for his intercession through the difficulties we've faced. Sometimes, when I look at his image on the candle beside me, I feel uncomfortable. I wonder whether my prayers are too concerned with earthly matters. I want financial relief. I want things repaired. I want our home to be beautiful. But more than any of those things, I want to grow closer to God. I want to receive His love and learn to share it. I want heavenly gains.

And perhaps that is where I have been misunderstanding holiness. Maybe being content doesn't mean never wanting anything. Maybe it means knowing that what I have, or what I lack, does not determine the fullness of my life. Maybe generosity doesn't require me to reject every comfort, but it does require me to notice when someone else is suffering and to respond as I reasonably can.

And maybe loving God first means allowing that love to influence not only how I pray, but how I spend, how I give, and how I live.

I keep returning to the widow and her little jar of oil. She did not wait until she had an abundance before she shared what she had. She gave from her need. And I think about the Philippians, who shared in Paul's distress. They did not simply tell him they cared. Their love became something tangible.

That is the kind of faith I want. Not a faith that makes me afraid to enjoy what God has given me, but one that keeps me from becoming so comfortable that I forget the needs of others.

I may still restore the backyard. We may eventually improve the driveway and make our home more beautiful. But I hope that as I do, I will continue asking whether I am making room in my life for someone else's needs. I hope I never become so concerned with what my home is missing that I forget to be grateful for the shelter it provides. And I hope that when I see someone living without that shelter, my concern becomes more than a passing sadness.

Today, Paul reminds me that contentment can be learned. Jesus reminds me that money must never become my master. And the woman in her car reminds me that love cannot remain merely a feeling.

Perhaps the question isn't whether I have too much or want too much. Perhaps it is whether I am learning to love enough. I don't know that I will ever answer that question perfectly, but I want to keep asking it.

Because when everything else is stripped away, the beauty of my home, the money in my accounts, the things I've gained and lost, none of those things can replace the love of God. And none of them can love my neighbor for me.

I want to be grateful for what I have, content with what I cannot have, and generous with what I can give. Perhaps that is where true abundance begins.
